title: Improving Human Verification of LLM Reasoning through Interactive Explanation Interfaces
venue: 31st International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '26)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether the way large language model (LLM) reasoning is presented affects people’s ability to understand and verify mathematical solutions, with particular relevance to educational uses such as tutoring and problem solving. The authors argue that standard chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations are often long, text-heavy, and hard for users to inspect for errors. The core research questions ask whether interactive explanation formats improve verification accuracy, reduce time and effort, and are preferred over traditional text-based outputs.

To address this, the authors designed three interactive explanation interfaces for LLM-generated math reasoning: interactive Chain-of-Thought (iCoT), interactive Program-of-Thought (iPoT), and interactive Graph (iGraph). All three formats preserve the underlying reasoning content but restructure it using features such as dual-panel layouts, problem summaries, color-coded variables, navigation/playback controls, pseudocode representations, or graph-based visualizations. The study used GSM8K math word problems with both correct explanations and systematically injected errors across nine error categories. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: traditional CoT, iCoT, iPoT, or iGraph.

The empirical study involved 125 undergraduate students from two U.S. universities in a controlled classroom setting, with the experiment delivered through a web-based platform hosted on HuggingFace Spaces. Each participant reviewed ten explanations and judged whether each was correct; for incorrect cases, they also identified the faulty step. The study collected quantitative outcomes such as verification accuracy, error localization accuracy, response time, and interaction logs, along with post-study Likert-scale survey responses and open-ended feedback about clarity, usability, engagement, and satisfaction.

The main conclusion is that interactive explanation interfaces improved human verification of LLM reasoning compared with standard CoT. iGraph produced the best overall performance, with the highest verification accuracy and error localization accuracy, and also the fastest average response times. iPoT and iCoT also outperformed traditional CoT on verification-related measures. Participants generally preferred the interactive formats over standard CoT, with iGraph rated highest for clarity and satisfaction and iPoT rated highly for engagement. The authors conclude that interactive, structured explanation interfaces can make AI reasoning easier to follow and audit in educational and human-AI collaboration contexts.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's large language model family used to generate mathematical reasoning explanations and interactive explanation interfaces.
identified_tools.use_case: Claude was used to generate GSM8K math explanations and render them into four formats: traditional CoT, interactive CoT (iCoT), interactive Program-of-Thought (iPoT), and interactive Graph (iGraph). Participants then used these Claude-generated explanations to judge correctness and identify erroneous steps.

findings.finding_summary: Across 125 participants reviewing Claude-generated GSM8K explanations, interactive explanation formats significantly improved verification accuracy over standard CoT. Verification accuracy was 85.6% for iGraph, 82.5% for iPoT, and 80.6% for iCoT, versus 73.5% for traditional CoT; Kruskal-Wallis H(3)=13.12, p=0.004, with pairwise Mann-Whitney tests showing significant advantages over CoT for iCoT (U=323.5, p=0.047, r=0.32), iPoT (U=306.0, p=0.023, r=0.38), and iGraph (U=221.5, p=0.003, r=0.51).
findings.measure: Verification accuracy on judging correctness of Claude-generated GSM8K math explanations
findings.effect_size: r=0.32 (iCoT vs CoT); r=0.38 (iPoT vs CoT); r=0.51 (iGraph vs CoT)

findings.finding_summary: Participants were better able to localize the exact erroneous step in Claude-generated explanations when using interactive formats. Wrong-step identification accuracy was 85.2% for iGraph, 80.1% for iPoT, and 79.3% for iCoT, compared with 66.1% for traditional CoT; Kruskal-Wallis H(3)=13.12, p=0.004, and Bonferroni-corrected pairwise Mann-Whitney tests found significant differences versus CoT for iCoT (U=300.8, p=0.045), iPoT (U=271.5, p=0.021), and iGraph (U=153.0, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Error localization / wrong-step identification accuracy on Claude-generated GSM8K explanations

findings.finding_summary: Participants using interactive interfaces responded faster on average to Claude-generated explanations, but pairwise differences were not statistically significant after correction. Mean response times were 57.9 seconds for iGraph, 59.5 seconds for iCoT, 60.1 seconds for iPoT, and 64.7 seconds for traditional CoT (with SDs 41.4, 35.8, 37.9, and 40.9 respectively); the overall Kruskal-Wallis test was H(3)=13.12, p=0.004.
findings.measure: Response time per question when verifying Claude-generated explanations

findings.finding_summary: Post-study survey results indicated users preferred the interactive formats for understanding and checking Claude-generated reasoning, with iGraph rated highest for understanding, error identification, and overall satisfaction, while iPoT received the highest engagement ratings. The paper reports that interactive formats were preferred over traditional CoT on general measures G1-G5 and that design features such as dual-panel layout, summaries, color coding, and step-by-step presentation were rated positively, especially for iGraph.
findings.measure: Post-study Likert-scale ratings of understanding, error identification, engagement, preference, and satisfaction

quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled between-subjects empirical study with random assignment across interface conditions and n=125, but it is not a classroom effectiveness trial and uses undergraduate participants completing verification tasks rather than direct K-12 learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported improvements in verification accuracy and error localization are substantial in magnitude (e.g., 73.5% to 85.6% accuracy; 66.1% to 85.2% error localization), indicating a meaningful positive impact on human verification of AI-generated math reasoning.
